headline: Ancient City Grew Richer by Spreading Wealth, Not Hoarding It
meta_description: A 4,000-year-old city defied history by becoming more equal as it prospered, focusing on shared infrastructure instead of palaces.
summary_short: Mohenjo-daro grew wealthier while becoming more equal—the opposite of what happened in ancient Egypt and Greece.
body:
A 4,000-year-old city in the Indus civilization became wealthier by sharing prosperity instead of concentrating it among rulers and elites. New research from the University of York examined Mohenjo-daro, the largest city of its time, and discovered that as the urban center matured and grew more productive, the gap between its richest and poorest households actually shrank. By the city's later years, the wealth divide had dropped to levels typical of the first farming villages—a pattern that directly contradicts the traditional historical assumption that inequality increases alongside economic growth.

Mohenjo-daro invested its resources in infrastructure that benefited everyone. The city built sophisticated brick-lined drains and organized street layouts rather than palaces, gold-filled tombs, or monuments to celebrate rulers. Indus seals, which were essential tools for trade and business, have been found in ordinary homes across the city rather than concentrated in the hands of a ruling class. This distribution suggests that commercial resources and authority were not monopolized by a single powerful leader. Instead, residents appear to have cooperated to ensure that households had broad access to what they needed for a comfortable life.

The city also maintained standardized weights and measures throughout the region, supporting fairer trade for merchants and residents alike. While ancient Egyptians were building pyramids for god-kings and Greeks were constructing massive palaces, the people of the Indus were building something entirely different: a thriving, productive society organized around shared needs. Dr. Adam Green notes that "in the period when inequality appears to be lowest, productivity appears to rise," offering a striking lesson for today. Mohenjo-daro demonstrates that an advanced urban society can be highly inventive and economically successful while distributing resources and power equitably.
quick_facts: Mohenjo-daro: largest city of the Indus civilization, 4,000 years old
Wealth gap narrowed as city matured, becoming equal to early farming villages
Indus seals found in ordinary homes, not royal palaces or elite buildings
Infrastructure focus: brick drains and streets instead of monuments to rulers
Standardized weights and measures supported fair trade across the region
